subject: Discovery recap: Finly - p95 latency & concurrency requirements
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Alex Chen <alex.chen@finly.com>
Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>, Dylan Brooks <dylan_brooks@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 12 May 2027 15:02:00 -0700
Subject: Discovery recap: Finly - p95 latency & concurrency requirements

Hi Alex —

Thanks again for taking the time today. Quick recap from our call and the things we captured as top priorities for Finly as you evaluate an inference partner: 

- Pain points we heard:
  - Checkout chatbot and document summarization flows are experiencing high tail latency during peak traffic, impacting merchant conversion.
  - Current vendor struggles with streaming UX — partial responses are arriving slowly which hurts user experience.
  - Cost per 1k messages is spiraling with current autoscaling strategy; want better unit economics at scale.

- Current stack:
  - Models: mix of open LLMs (7B and 13B variants) hosted via vendor-managed endpoints.
  - Frontend: streaming-enabled React UI that expects sub-200ms initial token latency for streaming start.
  - Traffic profile: steady baseline of ~400 QPS with 5-10 minute spikes up to ~1.8k QPS during promotions.

- Success criteria (what Finly needs):
  - p95 token latency for standard chat flows <= 350ms, and p95 end-to-end response <= 750ms for 99% of steady-state traffic.
  - Streaming start (time-to-first-token) consistently <200ms at target concurrency.
  - Sustained concurrent streams: support 800+ simultaneous streaming sessions without degradation; burst to 2k for short windows.
  - Clear cost model with predictable committed capacity and fallbacks.

- Next steps we agreed on:
  1) Redwood to share a short technical note with recommended config options (quantization, batching, prefix caching) + initial sizing estimate — ETA: 48 hours (Aditya/Dylan).
  2) Finly to provide anonymized request traces and a short list of representative prompts so we can run a targeted benchmark.
  3) Schedule a focused technical deep-dive (30-45m) with Finly infra and our runtime team next week.

I attached the Redwood datasheet and a doc with a few SLA/Q&A items we discussed. I also uploaded today’s recording.

Would you confirm that the p95/end-to-end targets above capture your goals? Anything to add on concurrency or burst patterns?

Best,
Marissa
Enterprise Sales | Redwood Inference
marissa_cole@redwood.com

Attachments: redwood-datasheet.pdf, finly_sla_questions.docx, call-recording.mp3
From: Alex Chen <alex.chen@finly.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 12 May 2027 17:30:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Discovery recap: Finly - p95 latency & concurrency requirements

Marissa —

Thanks for the clear summary, this is exactly what we discussed. A few clarifications from our side: 

- The p95/end-to-end numbers you listed look right. To be explicit: p95 token latency <= 350ms and p95 E2E <= 750ms for normal loads; during very short promotional spikes we can tolerate E2E up to ~1.2s but not for sustained periods.
- Our current telemetry shows that time-to-first-byte (TTFB) for streaming often hits 400-600ms under load, which is the main UX issue.
- Concurrency: the 800 concurrent streaming sessions is our medium-term target (next quarter). The bursts to 2k happen for 3-7 minutes during campaigns, roughly twice a month.

I’ll share a sanitized trace dump and 10 representative prompts by EOD tomorrow. Also looping in Procurement (procurement@finly.com) — they want a ballpark on committed capacity pricing before the next exec sync.

Appreciate the quick turnaround. Looking forward to the sizing note.

—Alex
Head of Product, Finly
From: Dylan Brooks <dylan_brooks@redwood.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>, Alex Chen <alex.chen@finly.com>
Date: Thu, 13 May 2027 08:15:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Discovery recap: Finly - p95 latency & concurrency requirements

Alex / Marissa —

Quick technical notes from our runtime team before we put together the sizing doc: 

- For the streaming UX requirement (TTFT <200ms), two levers are critical: eager partial-token flushes in the runtime and optimized batching windows (small, latency-aware batches for first tokens, larger batches for subsequent tokens).
- We recommend trying a 4-bit quantized 13B variant for the summarization/chat pipelines to reduce GPU latency and memory pressure; this will help hit p95 targets with lower cost.
- Prefix/KV cache: if you have repeated context across sessions (e.g., merchant config templates), enabling prefix caching can cut p95 by ~15-25% in our benchmarks.
- Initial sizing (very rough): to meet steady-state 800 concurrent streaming sessions with p95 E2E <= 750ms and time-to-first-token <200ms, estimated committed capacity is 6 dedicated GPU instances (A100-class equivalent) with adaptive burst headroom. For burst to 2k, we recommend autoscaling to a burst tier (spot-backed or preemptible) and an abort/fallback policy to a cheaper model variant for non-critical requests.

I’ll include these notes and sample config snippets in the doc Marissa will send out.

—Dylan
Runtime Engineer | Redwood Inference
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>

Alex —

I attached the datasheet and SLA question doc. If Procurement needs anything else for a preliminary commercial thread (SOW template, billing cadence), loop me in and I’ll pull the right folks.

Best,
